report:
## Conclusion

The claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes an increase in autism is **not supported by scientific evidence**. Multiple large, well-designed studies have specifically tested this "too many, too soon" hypothesis and found no association.

The key study directly testing cumulative vaccine/antigen exposure (DeStefano et al., 2013, *Journal of Pediatrics*) examined children with and without autism and found that increasing exposure to antibody-stimulating proteins and polysaccharides in vaccines during the first two years of life was **not associated** with increased risk of autism spectrum disorder, including autism with regression (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/).

A recent large cohort study of 1.2 million children similarly found no compelling evidence that childhood vaccines cause autism or other chronic conditions (https://www.healthline.com/health-news/research-finds-no-evidence-vaccines-cause-autism).

A comprehensive review in *ScienceDirect/PMC* ("The myth of vaccination and autism spectrum") synthesizes decades of evidence-based studies and concludes the scientific consensus firmly refutes causation between vaccines (including the number/schedule of vaccines) and autism (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8694782/).

I also note that in 2025 the CDC website was controversially revised to state the "vaccines do not cause autism" claim is "not evidence-based" — a change independently fact-checked and criticized as inconsistent with the actual body of scientific literature, which has failed to identify any plausible biological mechanism or epidemiological signal linking vaccine quantity/schedule to autism risk (https://www.factcheck.org/2025/11/revised-cdc-website-about-autism-and-vaccines-is-not-evidence-based/).

**Bottom line:** The scientific consensus, based on large epidemiological studies and biological plausibility research, is that increasing the number of childhood vaccines does not increase autism risk. This claim is false.
